title: What actually makes a game go viral?
author: BJGG69
selftext:
Before you say focus on the story/visuals/gameplay/promotion, I've seen some games with the most primitive graphics, or no storyline, without any promotion pick up thousands of plays. 

I am trying to build a personality based game (the ones that facebook was flooded with at some point where people click to find their persona), but its so hard to get people to play and actually share it. 

With so many things to focus on in the development process, whats the one item on the to-do list will contribute most to the virality of the game?

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body: Any way to make that happen without becoming even more broke than I already am?

comments.author: EliasWick
comments.body: All of the comments here mention something different, and they're all correct. Add Luck to the bucket of things you need too.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
The real big boys figured out that you can buy viral. Games like Clash of Clans spent like $1M a day in advertising to get $1.1M in revenue, netting a lot of money still, but the vitality was bought.

Games that go viral by themselves need an extremely good hook, which attracts non-players. Untitled Goose Game comes to mind. You see five seconds and think: I wanna play this.

The successful gacha games are not like that at all. They pay for ads and make just enough money to keep paying for those ads. As soon as the cost of an install drops below the average revenue, the game is dropped. Hypercasual was extremely notorious for this. For two months every ad is "Fridge Organizer", game made millions, and then was forgotten.

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body: If I had a million dollars I'd spend it on girls and shoes. Mike Posner lyrics aside, thanks for your comment, didn't know about the untitled goose game, and its visual immediately strikes the feeling of "I want to play this" which is genuinely hard to convey.

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body:
The point is that these guys turn 1 million into 2 million, repeatedly. That's way easier than turning nothing into 1 million.  
In the end, all of them have 1M to blow on girls and drugs.

comments.author: BansheeTheGame
comments.body: You’re talking about virality, but not whether you already have users. The problem is really three separate jobs: get a new player in, keep them engaged, and give them a reason to share. Have you run playtests yet? Do you know what your target audience actually enjoys and where they drop off?

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body:
I had a few of my friends test out the game and here is what they said:   
1) The idea in principle is very intriguing - make a fruit salad and it reveals your MBTI. During the tests, most of the readings came out wrong, so had to change it to a more generic personality description, which is not the same level of fun or wow factor, but at least its not outright wrong. 

  
2) The game itself is not intended to keep players locked for prolonged periods of time, instead the virality relies on people sharing the test results, but so far nobody wants to refer it, cause I guess it looks kinda ugly, instead of the intended cute look.    


3) I am reworking the visuals so that the game feels more aesthetically pleasing to make people more inclined to share it, but wanted to make sure if that's the right place to invest all the effort or if there is something I am missing.

replies.author: BansheeTheGame
replies.body: Try an open playtest with people recruited from Reddit. That should quickly show whether the concept has any organic sharing potential. Friends are useful for early feedback, but they’re invested in you, so they’re not a reliable signal for virality.

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body: Never mentioned making money - I only wanted more people to have the shared experience of playing the game

comments.author: LastJoker96
comments.body:
I think that the most important factor is having fun!  
At the end of the day, most people forget (game devs more than players imho) that we are talking about "Games". I'm going to be 30 yo soon, and as far as i remember, before the "tech era", when we were just children on the streets, we used to invent games on the go, just to have a blast of fun. All we had was a ball, some toys (soldiers, animals, superheroes figures, collectibles cards) and we were calling it a day just by changing some rules of a pre-existing game, or some stuff that was just...simple! I was thinking about (and maybe re-realizing) this some days ago, and all of a sudden i just stopped working on all my previous game projects, as i had a new idea which is just fun!  
Not complicated, not hard to develop, not hard to understand for the player, just funny!  
Of course if depends on what you are looking to achieve, but for a game to be "viral", imo fun (and the right dose of luck) is the most important factor!  
Some examples are party games like Among Us,Mecha Chameleon, Liar's Bar, and so on!  
No plot, no fancy animations, nothing like that. One or two simple mechanics, and the rest is just pure fun!

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
There's two paths. One is just making a really good game, people then see YouTubers playing it and word gets around.

The second is making a game that a YouTuber can make look fun even if it isn't. There's many games now that are essentially meme slop games. Low effort games that usually have a single gimmick and often extremely jank. 

We've really started to move away from YouTubers reviewing games, especially YouTubers aiming their channel at the younger generations. They are more like influencers and will try and make even the shitist games seem fun and entertaining.

Either way one takes a lot of work and dedication with no guarantees and the other is a complete gamble where 99.9% of these low effort games aren't going to go "viral" even sell.

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body:
>There's many games now that are essentially meme slop games.

Agreed 100% on this. And sometimes it can be a little discouraging to see developers pouring their soul into the game getting 100 plays, while some trolls having a million

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
Exactly. It's especially prevalent in the VR space at the moment. 

We also had the whole simulator slop era too which seems to have died down a bit now thankfully.

Places like Steam still vet spammed with these type of games though. You have some people or game studios pumping games like these out every few weeks in the hope one might go viral. Unfortunately that practice is only going to increase with AI too.

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body:
It probably doesn't sound authentic, but advertising. I knew this guy who made the shittiest records you ever heard, but he put it out everywhere, had TV and internet ads, walked around giving samples of the album, got in touch with advertisers and made generational wealth from it.

But, regardless if you advertise or not, a hit is when you make something innovative, or stupidly fun. It just has to be something functionally sound. So my advice is not to make a clone, but make something different, which stands out. Fez is a good example of outside thinking. Despite the bad press surrounding the developer, Fez was innovative enough to be a standout innovation. 

Why has no one done **kemon with aliens and if they did why has no one heard of it?

comments.author: Middle-Lab-2107
comments.body: Learn how to code, line by line. Learn how to solve problems. Then develop the game. Entirely on your own. Put your blood sweat and tears into it. Ditch AI. That's a good start
